claims.text: HEBM at 400 rpm for 4 hours with cooling intervals, followed by SPS at 1100 °C and 30 MPa for 10 minutes, is an applicable processing route for CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed HEBM–SPS process will produce greater than 98% theoretical density.
The proposed process will produce grains 200–500 nm in size.
The resulting structure will be a dominant FCC solid solution containing approximately 10–15 vol% BCC phase.
Rapid SPS heating and a short dwell suppress diffusion-controlled HCP nucleation associated with Ti-rich segregation.
The high defect density generated by HEBM promotes formation of a metastable FCC/BCC solid solution.
Dual-phase stability is maximized within a sintering-temperature window of 1050–1150 °C.
Dual-phase stability is maximized at an effective sintering strain rate of approximately 10^-3–10^-2 s^-1.
The effective sintering strain rate is driven by thermal-expansion mismatch and particle rearrangement.
The specified operating regime maximizes Ti solute drag on dislocations while preventing HCP nucleation.
Ti is kinetically trapped in the FCC lattice or partitions into a minor BCC phase because of rapid cooling and solute drag.
The processed alloy will have a Vickers hardness of 650–750 HV.
The hardness increase is caused jointly by Hall–Petch grain refinement and solid-solution strengthening by Ti and the other constituent elements.
The processed alloy will exceed 800 MPa tensile strength while retaining elongation above 20%.
Conventional casting of CoCrFeNiTi produces a porous, homogeneous single-phase structure with hardness near 200 HV.
Sintering above 1200 °C or dwelling longer than 20 minutes permits enough diffusion for HCP nucleation and causes the strategy to fail.
Insufficient milling energy produces inadequate defect density, incomplete homogenization, and phase segregation.
Ti may form a minor HCP phase at grain boundaries despite rapid sintering, reducing ductility.
Vickers hardness can be tested using a 500 g load and a 15-second dwell.
Low hardness despite a nanocrystalline grain size would imply that grain refinement is not the operative strengthening mechanism and that a soft phase or porosity is responsible.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis states a heating rate of 100 °C/min for SPS, whereas the intervention and conditions specify 100 °C/min only at low temperature and 50 °C/min at higher temperature.

The mechanism attributes hardness to both grain refinement and solid-solution strengthening, but the falsification rule treats low hardness at small grain size as evidence against grain refinement without independently controlling or measuring solute strengthening, phase softness, and porosity.
